strengths: Presents a genuinely novel theoretical framework for transfer learning in infinite-width, feature-learning (mean-field/µP) two-layer neural networks, extending beyond prior NTK/proportional-limit theories that either lack feature learning or require Gaussian-equivalence assumptions.

Develops two complementary and mutually consistent formalisms (a Bayesian/replica-based theory and a DMFT gradient-flow theory), both leading to adaptive kernel predictors that explicitly depend on source and target task statistics via an elastic coupling parameter δ.

Careful and thorough positioning relative to closely related prior work (e.g., Ingrosso et al., Shan et al., Tahir et al.), clearly articulating what is technically new (non-Gaussian, non-perturbative kernel adaptation even in the P=Θ(N) regime).

Strong empirical validation: theory predictions (dashed lines) closely match simulations (solid lines) from Langevin dynamics and gradient descent across many settings (linear regression, polynomial/Hermite teacher tasks, CIFAR-10/Fashion-MNIST/MNIST classification, and a CNN extension in the appendix).

Rich and intuitive phenomenology is uncovered and explained: interplay between elastic coupling, feature-learning richness (γ0), task similarity, and target dataset size, including interesting non-monotonic/asymmetric effects when transferring from lower-to-higher or higher-to-lower complexity tasks.
Detailed and self-contained appendix derivations (replica computation, saddle-point equations, DMFT field equations) supporting reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: The theory and most experiments are restricted to two-layer networks; the paper does not address how these results extend to deep networks, which limits direct relevance to practical transfer learning settings where deep architectures dominate.

Real-data experiments are relatively small-scale and simplified (binary class-pair problems on CIFAR-10/Fashion-MNIST/MNIST with very small target sample sizes and grayscale/downsampled inputs), so it is unclear how well the theory's qualitative predictions would generalize to realistic transfer-learning workloads or modern architectures (e.g., ResNets, transformers).

The theory does not average over the data distribution (acknowledged explicitly as a limitation), so the resulting equations scale with the number of datapoints and do not yield clean closed-form predictions for generalization as a function of P2 and task alignment in the way some prior spectral-bias theories do.

Some qualitative explanations (e.g., the grokking-like conjecture behind the high-to-low degree polynomial transfer results in Fig. 5) are offered somewhat speculatively without rigorous theoretical support beyond intuition.

The connection to practical fine-tuning methods (e.g., low-rank adaptation such as LoRA) is only briefly discussed as future work despite being highly relevant to current transfer-learning practice, somewhat limiting the paper's practical significance.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, which may limit accessibility to a broader ML audience outside the statistical-mechanics/mean-field theory community; the main text often relies heavily on appendix derivations for full understanding.

strengths: Develops two complementary and technically careful theoretical frameworks (Bayesian/aNBK posterior and DMFT gradient-flow dynamics) for transfer learning in feature-learning infinite-width two-layer networks, extending prior single-task theories (e.g., Lauditi et al. aNBK, Bordelon & Pehlevan DMFT) to a two-task elastic-coupling setting.

The derivations are detailed and largely self-contained, with extensive appendix work (replica computation, saddle-point equations, Schur-complement simplifications for linear networks, CNN extension) that appears internally consistent.

The theory is validated against simulations (Langevin dynamics and gradient descent on moderately wide networks, N~5000-20000) across a reasonable range of settings: linear regression, polynomial/Hermite teacher-student tasks, and real image data (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, MNIST), with good qualitative and quantitative agreement.

The paper surfaces interesting and somewhat non-trivial phenomenology: the interaction between elastic coupling, feature-learning richness (γ0), task similarity, and target dataset size, including asymmetric effects of transfer from high-to-low vs low-to-high complexity tasks, and a connection to fine-tuning/linear probing as limiting cases.

Related work section is thorough, carefully situating the contribution relative to proportional-limit Bayesian transfer theories and other mean-field frameworks, clarifying where this work's predictions diverge (non-vanishing transfer effect in the P/N→0 limit).
weaknesses: The empirical validation, while broad, remains at toy scale: only two-layer networks, binary/few-class classification with very small P1/P2 (tens to a few thousand), grayscale-downsampled 28x28 images, and small single-dataset ablations — this limits confidence that the theory's qualitative conclusions generalize to realistic transfer learning regimes (deep networks, larger/more diverse datasets, more than two classes).

The paper claims qualitative differences from existing Bayesian transfer-learning theories (e.g., Ingrosso et al. [40], Shan et al. [41], Tahir et al. [42]) but never empirically or numerically contrasts its predictions against these alternative theories/baselines — the comparison is only narrative, which weakens the significance claim.

Restriction to two-layer networks is a substantial limitation (acknowledged by the authors) since most practical transfer learning concerns deep, often pretrained, architectures; it is unclear how much of the phenomenology (e.g., elastic coupling tradeoffs) would survive or change in deeper nets.

The real-dataset experiments (Sec 3.3) are fairly shallow in analysis — mostly single test-loss-vs-δ curves and qualitative preactivation-distribution plots, without deeper quantitative dissection (e.g., systematic sweep over task similarity for images, statistical significance, comparison to standard fine-tuning baselines such as full fine-tuning vs. linear probing in practice).

The theory does not average over datasets (finite-P equations), explicitly noted as a limitation, which restricts the predictive/generalization claims to specific realized datasets rather than population-level statements, reducing the generality of the 'theory predicts generalization' claims.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy even in the main text (e.g., Results 1 and 2 with many order parameters, non-standard GP conditioning), which may hinder accessibility and broader impact outside a narrow theoretical-physics-of-learning audience.
No code/data release or explicit reproducibility statement is provided despite fairly intricate saddle-point/DMFT numerics required to reproduce results.

Significance to the broader ML community is somewhat unclear: the elastic-weight-coupling formalism and many qualitative conclusions (richer source helps more when aligned; more data compensates for less coupling) are intuitive and have analogues in prior transfer-learning theory/practice, so the incremental conceptual novelty beyond combining known techniques (aNBK + DMFT + Franz-Parisi-style elastic coupling) is moderate.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: prior Bayesian/NTK-based transfer learning theories lose feature learning in the overparameterized limit, while this work develops a mean-field/µP theory where both source and target tasks exhibit genuine feature learning.

Provides two complementary and mutually consistent theoretical frameworks (Bayesian aNBK posterior and DMFT gradient flow with weight decay), both yielding adaptive kernel predictors governed by an elastic coupling parameter δ.

Extensive and careful analytical derivations (replica calculation, saddle-point equations, special cases for linear networks with whitened/correlated data, decoupled vs. shared data) that give interpretable closed-form limits (e.g., recovering NNGP/lazy limits at δ=0,γ0=0, and full feature reuse at δ→∞).

Strong empirical validation: theory is compared against finite but wide (N=20000) network simulations (Langevin dynamics and gradient descent/DMFT) across linear regression, polynomial/Hermite teacher-student tasks, and image classification (CIFAR-10, Fashion-MNIST, MNIST), with generally good agreement.

Reveals genuinely interesting and nontrivial phenomenology: optimal interplay between elastic coupling, feature-learning richness, task similarity, and dataset size; asymmetric effects of transfer from low-to-high vs. high-to-low complexity tasks; connections to fine-tuning/linear-probing special cases.

Appendices include a thoughtful discussion contrasting this approach with related proportional-limit Bayesian transfer learning works (Ingrosso et al., Shan et al.), clarifying technical differences (mean-field vs. NTK parameterization, absence of Gaussian equivalence assumption).
weaknesses: The theory and most clean analytical results are restricted to two-layer networks; extension to deeper networks (where transfer learning is arguably most practically relevant) is left to future work.

Real-data experiments are relatively small-scale and simplified (binary classification on small subsets of CIFAR-10/Fashion-MNIST, grayscale downsampling to 28x28, small P2), which somewhat limits the strength of claims about applicability to "real datasets."

The theory does not average over the data distribution, so equations scale with the number of datapoints rather than giving closed-form generalization curves as in some related spectral-bias theories (acknowledged as a limitation).

The exposition is extremely dense and notation-heavy (many order parameters, replica computations, inconsistent symbol usage between γ0/δ and η in some figures/appendix sections), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for readers outside the specific statistical-mechanics tradition.

No direct quantitative comparison or benchmarking against the closest prior transfer-learning theories (e.g., Ingrosso et al. 2025, Tahir et al. 2024) beyond qualitative discussion, making it harder to assess the practical added value of the new framework.
The CNN extension is only briefly sketched in the appendix with a single illustrative figure, so the generality claim to more realistic architectures remains largely unexplored.

Some practical implications (e.g., for LoRA-style or partial fine-tuning, deeper architectures) are left as speculative future work rather than demonstrated, somewhat limiting the immediate practical significance of the contribution.

strengths: Develops a comprehensive and technically rigorous DMFT-based theory of transfer learning in infinite-width, feature-learning (mu-P/mean-field) neural networks, extending prior single-task feature-learning theories to the two-stage (pretrain/fine-tune or jointly rich) setting.

Provides closed-form, interpretable results in tractable special cases (linear networks, population vs. finite source data, ultra-rich pretraining) that cleanly explain when transfer learning helps or hurts as a function of data amounts (P1, P2), source/target alignment, and feature-learning strength (gamma1, gamma2).

Strong agreement between theoretical DMFT predictions and numerical simulations of finite-but-wide networks (both synthetic polynomial tasks and real datasets such as CIFAR-10), across multiple figures, lending credibility to the theory.

Careful and thorough derivations (path-integral/DMFT for both gradient-flow and Bayesian posterior settings) are included in extensive appendices, making the work reproducible in principle and mathematically self-contained (including a helpful DMFT primer).

Good positioning relative to a large and relevant body of related work (Bayesian transfer learning, NTK/proportional-limit theories, continual learning), with explicit discussion of how this work's mu-P treatment differs from and extends prior Bayesian NTK-based transfer-learning theories.

Identifies non-trivial, somewhat counter-intuitive phenomena (e.g., negative transfer from finite-sample noise, harm from ultra-rich pretraining, asymmetry between easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy curricula) that are of practical interest beyond the toy models.
weaknesses: The exactly-solvable results are largely restricted to two-layer (shallow) linear or simple nonlinear networks with isotropic Gaussian data; deeper networks are acknowledged to have non-Markovian dynamics that are not solved, and the isotropic-data assumption limits applicability to realistic structured data.

For the finite-data fine-tuning result (Result 3) and its nonlinear/real-data extension, the key constants (c1, c2, c3) are not derived in closed form but left as free parameters, with only an ad hoc large-gamma1 ansatz used to compare against real datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10), weakening the rigor of the empirical validation in the most practically relevant regime.

Real-data experiments are limited in scope (two-layer ReLU MLPs on small binary-class subsets of CIFAR-10, N=20000, relatively small P1/P2), so it is unclear how well the qualitative conclusions generalize to deeper architectures, multi-class settings, or larger-scale data regimes typical of modern transfer learning.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation and lengthy derivations (much of the technical content relegated to a very long appendix), which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by non-specialist readers.

While the theory yields many qualitative phase-diagram-type conclusions, some practically important quantities (e.g., precise conditions for the sign of crosstalk/noise effects in general alignment settings) are only worked out in special cases (e.g., alpha_s=1, alpha_g=0), limiting the immediate practical predictive power of the theory.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored theoretical gap: prior infinite-width theories of transfer learning (NNGP/NTK, kernel-task alignment) assume fixed representations, while this work attempts to capture genuine feature learning on both source and target tasks via mean-field/µP DMFT.

The derivation connecting adaptive NTK kernels after rich pretraining to fine-tuning generalization (Results 2-4) yields interpretable closed-form predictions (e.g., rank-one spiked kernels, dependence on alignment α, data ratios ν1/ν2) that are genuinely novel contributions to the transfer-learning theory literature.

Reasonably thorough related-work positioning relative to NTK-proportional-limit Bayesian transfer learning (Ingrosso et al., Shan et al.) and deep linear fine-tuning theories (Tahir et al.), clarifying differences in parameterization and resulting predictions.

Some empirical validation is provided across a spectrum of settings — linear teacher/student, polynomial (Hermite) multi-index tasks, and small-scale real image classification (CIFAR-10) — with reasonably good agreement between DMFT/Bayesian theory predictions and finite-width simulations.

Identifies intuitive and practically relevant phenomena, such as negative transfer from finite pretraining data, non-monotonic optimal feature-learning strength, and easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy curriculum asymmetries.
weaknesses: The claimed 'general theory' for deep multi-layer feature-learning transfer (Section 2.1, Appendix B) is acknowledged to be analytically intractable ('quite complex,' 'non-Markovian') and is never solved or validated against experiments; essentially all concrete results (Results 1-4) are restricted to two-layer networks, so the paper's generality claims are oversold relative to what is actually delivered.

The quantitative (average-case) results rely on strong simplifying assumptions — isotropic Gaussian inputs, linear or low-degree polynomial teacher functions, MSE loss — that make it unclear how much of the derived phenomenology (e.g., exact rank-one/low-rank kernel structure, closed-form loss expressions) would survive under realistic, structured, or heavy-tailed data, which the authors themselves flag as a limitation but do not address.

Real-data experiments are narrow and small-scale (binary CIFAR-10 subsets with P2 as low as 200, two-layer ReLU nets), offering only qualitative/illustrative support rather than rigorous empirical validation of the theory's quantitative predictions across diverse architectures, tasks, or dataset scales.

The paper's results (Results 1-4, Sections 3.1-3.3, plus the Bayesian analysis in Appendices E/F) feel like a loosely connected collection of special cases (population limit, finite-sample linear regime, ultra-rich limit, Bayesian elastic-coupling variant) rather than a unified theory; the connections between these pieces and their relative importance are not always made clear in the main text.

Presentation and clarity are weak for a main-text research paper: heavy reliance on DMFT/path-integral machinery with minimal intuition-building in the main text, very dense notation introduced across Results 1-4 without consistent definitions, and most of the actual technical substance (derivations, DMFT actions, saddle-point equations) is relegated to a ~35-page appendix, making the core paper read more like a highly compressed technical summary than a self-contained contribution.

No direct empirical or theoretical comparison against competing transfer-learning theories discussed in related work (e.g., Tahir et al. 2024, Ingrosso et al. 2025, Aminian et al. 2024), despite the paper positioning itself relative to them; it is unclear whether the proposed framework yields materially different or better predictions in overlapping regimes.

Some conclusions (e.g., 'ultra-rich pretraining is always harmful', 'data-rich pretraining always helps') are stated as general takeaways but are proven only under narrow linear/isotropic assumptions with specific alignment conditions (e.g., αg=0), limiting the strength and generality of the paper's headline claims.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored theoretical question of transfer learning in the feature-learning (not static-kernel) infinite-width regime
Clean regime decomposition (population limit, finite source data, ultra-rich pretraining) yielding interpretable, falsifiable predictions about when transfer helps or hurts
Rigorous DMFT/path-integral derivations with extensive, self-contained appendices including a Bayesian extension via Franz-Parisi potential
Good breadth of empirical validation spanning linear toy models, polynomial tasks with nonlinear networks, and real CIFAR-10 experiments with close DMFT-to-GD agreement
Identifies and rigorously derives the phenomenon of 'representation overfitting'/negative transfer due to finite source data, a valuable and intuitive insight
Thorough related work situating the contribution clearly relative to NTK-based and Bayesian proportional-limit transfer learning theories
weaknesses: Rigorous quantitative results are largely restricted to linear/two-layer models; deeper and fully nonlinear settings are validated only numerically/qualitatively
Key constants (c1, c2, c3) in Result 3 are left implicit from DMFT saddle-point equations; real-dataset matching relies on an unprincipled ansatz for these constants
Reliance on isotropic/Gaussian data assumptions limits confidence that conclusions transfer to structured or heavy-tailed real data
Real-data experiments are relatively small-scale (2-class CIFAR-10 subsets), leaving broader empirical generalizability underexplored
Dense, symbol-heavy notation across many overlapping parameters (gamma0, gamma1, gamma2, nu1, nu2, chi, c1-c3, alpha_s, alpha_g) reduces accessibility
The jointly-rich (both-tasks feature learning) setting is validated mainly via qualitative trend-matching rather than precise quantitative metrics
